speechtext:
As my hon. friend pursues these
purely legal questions I always follow his legal arguments with a great deal of interest.
After it was all over the minister almost offered me a job in his law office, but I could not qualify. I think he just wanted to get me out of here. The minister went on:
Perhaps it is not necessary for me to say that the Minister of Finance has received a formal opinion from the deputy minister of justice that this is what is known as a continuing vote. From year to year the estimates are filled with items of this kind, including a number of pension items, which are voted once in an appropriation bill but which continue as a statutory charge. I used to lecture in the law faculty of McGill before I entered public life, but I have given up that occupation for the time being. If my hon. friend would like further elucidation I am sure the deputy minister of justice would be only too happy to discuss it with him. I can assure him that there is appropriate legal authority for the continuing payment of this item from year to year.
Well, I am a persistent sort of so-and-so, and I did not let it drop there. I suppose someone will cay that I should have taken the minister's suggestion and got in touch with

The Budget-Mr. Knowles the deputy minister of justice, but I made my own decision in the matter; I wrote a letter to the Auditor General and called his attention to the statements as they appeared in Hansard of December 10, asking whether he cared to make any comment and also whether or not this matter had ever been the subject of comment in a report of the Auditor General. Well, the Auditor General, who after all is a servant of parliament and not of the government, quite properly replied to my letter and dealt with the points I had raised. He gave me his comments and enclosed a copy of one of his reports, also a copy of a memorandum he had prepared dealing with this particular question. I find that despite the assurance the Minister of Finance gave me that the deputy minister of justice was quite sure this was all right, the Auditor General does question the practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware that the Auditor General, though a very distinguished public servant, is not a member of the legal profession.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Dare I say that might be in his favour? At any rate the point I am making just now is that he is appointed as a servant of parliament; and his function, as he clearly says in one of his letters to me, is to make sure that the authority of parliament in the voting of money is not overridden. Mr. Sellar called my attention to the Auditor General's report of 1947-48, at pages 15 and 16, where he has a section of about four paragraphs under the heading "Legislating by appropriation acts." This is a bit lengthy and a bit technical, but the gist of it is that he questions the practice of legislating by means of putting items in the estimates. In the first part of this section he says:
Since this office was established seventy years ago attention has, from time to time, been drawn to problems associated with legislating by means of token items in annual appropriation acts. For example, the procedure by-passes normal parliamentary safeguards against hasty decisions with respect to public expenditure. Further, the practice tends to disturb constitutional usages with respect to money bills-both within the House of Commons and in relationships between the Senate and the house. An ancillary characteristic is that the practice presents difficulties to searchers for the authority for payments.
Then he goes on in a rather lengthy paragraph, No. 40, to deal with a certain incident having to do with annuity payments, pointing out that the Auditor General had withheld the audit certificate in a certain case because the vote in the estimates seemed to override the provisions of the act, and the result was that one item after another, differently worded, was put in until finally by that means the government got its way. Then in paragraph 41 he deals with the matter by

pointing out that an illustration of this business of legislating by items in the estimates is the motorcar allowance to ministers, the Speakers of both houses, and the leader of the official opposition. Finally he concludes this section by saying:
The practice of legislating by appropriation acts has attractions when dealing with special cases or making temporary exceptions from general legislation: but the thought presents itself that it might be a safeguard and a convenience to members were such items listed together in a special schedule and the reasons therefor printed with each item-as is the practice with respect to bills.
I am going to bring forward other examples in just a moment; I am not dealing only with the motorcar allowance. That is just the example I happened to start with. The point I wish to make is that the Auditor General, who is not a lawyer and therefore does not go to the extent of saying whether such and such is illegal, does say that the practice of legislating by putting items in the estimates has attractions when dealing with special cases or making temporary exceptions from general legislation. You can hardly call it a temporary exception, however, to continue paying a $2,000 motorcar allowance from 1931 right down to 1950. The point the Auditor General makes, and the point I make, is that here we are paying out every year a sum of money which was never authorized by parliament in the way in which normal legislation is passed. The normal practice in connection with a money bill is that it is preceded by a resolution and goes through all the various stages. Before we got old age pensions it had to be done in that way. Before we got family allowances it was done in that way. Before we could get any increase in the old age pension it had to be done in that way. Before any money bill becomes law it has to go through all the processes and steps required for the enactment of legislation. When you can slip an item into the estimates and get it passed, however, to use the words of the Auditor General, you by-pass the normal procedures of parliament.
That is done in two ways. It is done by these continuing votes, such as the one that was passed in 1931 having to do with the motorcar allowance to cabinet ministers, the two Speakers, and the leader of the opposition. The result in that case is that it was just passed once in the simplest way possible, and from then on we do not even vote it; it is just listed in the estimates as statutory, and the Auditor General says many such items are scattered through the estimates. In other words, in many cases where the letter (S) appears in the estimates, the item is statutory only in the sense that once upon a time it was passed under the terms of a continuing vote, such as the one I have read

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a statute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a moment; your quarrel over this matter is with the Auditor General. In most cases where the letter (S) appears in the estimates it means to us that a proper money bill, a proper statute, has been passed by this house. When we see the letter (S) opposite the amount to be voted for old age pensions, or opposite the amount to be voted for family allowances or for disability pensions, we know that provision has been voted by parliament by means of a proper bill with all the terms and conditions set out in that statute. Now, however, we discover that in many cases in the estimates the (S) simply means that it was passed as a continuing item some time in the past. Then there are some cases, like the salary and motorcar allowance of the ministers, where you get two different kinds of votes grouped together. The Salaries Act provides for the $10,000; item 352 in the estimates of 1931 is taken to provide the other $2,000. Now in the estimates, however, they are conveniently put together as $12,000 and marked "Statutory".
Mr. Abbot!: My hon. friend used the phrase "a proper bill." What does he consider a proper bill?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A proper bill legislating for a particular purpose is a bill that stands on its own feet, so you can deal with the principle involved in that bill and so parliament can pass upon its terms and conditions. That is the criticism the Auditor General offers. As a matter of fact, it is the criticism that was made in a report coming from a committee of the Senate thirty years ago, more or less, which I will not take time to read simply because my own time is likely to run out on me.
I shall come back to this if I have time, but I wanted to say that the other way in which we are called upon to legislate by means of items in the estimates is through the inclusion of many items which we do vote every year but which have never been made proper, which have never been clearly set out in an act of parliament.
I can give a few examples. As a matter of fact I have before me a list of about twenty. There is an item in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture which provides for making certain appointments notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act. In other words by that vote we by-pass the normal requirements of the Civil Service Act, or the necessity of amending that act in the proper way. Oddly enough, there is an item in the section of the estimates headed "civil service commission"
The Budget-Mr. Knowles which provides for the payment of $2,000 a year extra to each of the three civil service commissioners. In view of the care with which the civil service commission carries on in dealing with salary matters, I am amazed that the three commissioners should accept salaries made up of certain amounts provided by statute, plus $2,000 each voted in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which is also provided by statute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is voted in the estimates each year, with the phrase "notwithstanding any of the provisions of the Civil Service Act." Then under external affairs there are three items that have such provisions. One has to do with the making of a large number of appointments all over the world, which are made notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act. We are proud of the fact that the civil service has reached the point it has in our modern democracy, yet we by-pass it time and again. Not only does the government by-pass the act; it bypasses the accepted procedure of changing an act by bringing in an amending bill. This is being done simply by placing an item in the estimates.
There is another external affairs item which has to do with the use of inconvertible foreign currencies to acquire property. Another has to do with the salary of the chairman of the joint United States-Canadian defence board. No statute has been passed to provide that salary; it is done simply by an item in the estimates. The same is true, as the minister knows, of the grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes, though I understand the intention is to bring in a proper statute with respect to that appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not a continuing appropriation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I have already made it clear that there are two ways in which this questionable practice is carried on, one by a continuing appropriation, the other by an appropriation every year which nevertheless by-passes the necessity and desirability of a statute. The secretary to the governor general, a good friend of mine-which proves that there is nothing personal in this-gets his salary in part under the statute, but largely through an item in the estimates containing the provision that this is done notwithstanding the provisions of the governing statute. There are two such items in the estimates of the Department of Justice and one in the estimates of the Department of Labour. There are a couple in the section known as legislation. One of them in particular is the extra $4,000 per year paid to our

The Budget-Mr. Knowles good friends the parliamentary assistants. There never has been a statute to provide for the payment of that money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has been, each year. I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but he must be accurate. That money is voted each year, and it is in the Appropriation Act each year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If it is of any interest to the Minister of Finance I can tell him that my notes are taken from a memorandum I received from the Auditor General himself in response to an inquiry I addressed to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I said before, the Auditor General is a distinguished public servant, but he is not a member of the legal profession and his views are his own.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly they are, but I-happen to agree with him. The minister and the government do not hesitate to quote the Auditor General or any distinguished public servant when he is on their side. In this instance I want to make it perfectly clear that he is not saying what has been done is illegal. He is questioning the practice and suggesting that a change should be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My only reason for interrupting was that the hon. member said these were not authorized by statute. I am convinced that the Auditor General never said to my hon. friend or anyone else that the $4,000 a year paid the parliamentary assistants is not authorized by statute. I am sure my hon. friend will not find that in any memorandum from the Auditor General or anyone else.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Auditor General includes that item in the list of twenty or more which he gives as examples of vote texts that legislate, and he seriously questions the practice of legislating merely by putting items in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend's travelling expenses are in exactly the same category.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The travelling expenses that are paid to us when the government puts an item in the estimates to cover our trip home at Easter are in that category.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The expenses that are paid to us on a statutory basis to cover our coming down here at the first of the session and going home at the end are provided for in the proper way by statute. Similarly, if we are going to pass a supplementary item every year providing for the full payment of the indemnity of members of the House of Commons and Senators who have been absent owing to illness, the same Auditor General suggests that, now that it has become a

recognized practice, it should be done by amending the Senate and House of Commons Act. This is not an original idea of mine. That is what the Auditor General has said quite clearly in his memorandum; he has said that the Senate and House of Commons Act should be amended to take care of these things that are being done year in and year out instead of doing them by means of these annual votes on the estimates.
In that connection he points out that the matter was the subject of discussion at one time in the British house, and as a result of a rather interesting case, which was known as the Australian case, Fisher v. the Queen (1903) A.C. 158, the judicial committee of the privy council ruled that an appropriation act could not override a statute. Consequently in 1908, quite a while ago, the British public accounts committee abandoned its previous viewpoint, which was that appropriation acts could be used in the way that we are using them here, and they declared:
It is desirable in the interests of financial regularity and constitutional consistency that such a procedure should be resorted to as rarely as possible, and only to meet a temporary emergency.
And:
The fact that a proposed vote overrides an existing statute should be clearly stated on the face of the estimate, with the reasons for adopting that course, so that no doubt can exist of the deliberate intention of parliament. The exceptional nature of the vote should also be indicated in the Appropriation Act.
I was in the midst of giving certain examples when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) interrupted me. There is in the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys an item that permits of certain funds to be paid to civil servants, notwithstanding the provisions of the relevant statute. In the Department of National Defence there are a couple of large items, to which the Auditor General calls attention, which provide for commitments to be made in future years that total over $600 million. The Auditor General has put it mildly and I agree with him. He questions the practice of agreeing to these large appropriations by the simple process of an item in the estimates as distinct from the normal money bill procedure that requires all the stages that we go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend call an appropriation bill a money bill?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly it is a money bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the money bill of all money bills.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But it includes well over $2 billion worth of separate items, and we have

no chance of voting upon the principle involved in these various expenditures in the way in which expenditures are supposed to be dealt with by the process of a resolution and a bill going through all its stages. The minister knows about this because I am sure this memorandum is available to him, as it was to me-as it certainly should be-and all of the quotations and the citations are here for him to read.
I submit seriously that it is not just a technicality. Perhaps the government is trying to save time; but I think they have been in power so long and feel that their power is so great that they follow the simplest course of putting an item in the estimates instead of first bringing down a bill. That is the way it has been done so far with these grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes. That is the way it has been done for several years now with respect to the national health grants which come under the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I sat in the gallery of the Manitoba legislature a week or so ago and heard the minister of health there tell Lloyd Stinson, who had asked him a question, that he understood there soon was going to be a statute so that the provinces would know where they stand with respect to the health grants. I hope that will be done soon, because I make it clear that I am not against this money being voted; I am for it. In fact, I am for a great deal more of it. But I want it done in the proper way. Under Trade and Commerce there is an item of this nature. There is one under Transport and also one under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Another one to which the Auditor General calls particular attention is an item in the Finance estimates of this year, vote No. 101, which reads as follows:
To provide, subject to the approval of the treasury board, for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen expenses, including recoverable advances for working capital purposes, and for the re-use of any sum repaid to this appropriation from other appropriations.
From that the Auditor General went on to discuss the question of motorcar allowances and all these other items that are put through in this simple way rather than in the slightly more roundabout but clear-cut way that is provided. The Auditor General has made it clear to me in the correspondence that I have had with him-and I have written him on several occasions-that he is not interested, and that officially he is not supposed to be interested, in the legal aspects of it. I do not quarrel with the practice of the Minister of Finance in going to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or to the deputy minister of justice for his legal opinions. The Auditor
The Budget-Mr. Knowles General makes it quite clear that it is his function as a servant of parliament to help parliament to protect its interests in the voting of money. One of the principles that have been laid down in our parliamentary institution is that the voting of money is left to parliament and that, before these permanent and continuing sums of money are paid, there should be a statute that provides for the payment of that money, and lays down the terms and conditions under which it is paid.
I think I should take just a moment to read something I referred to a moment ago but did not read because I was afraid of the running out of my time. It was a part of a report made to the Senate by a special committee of the Senate on the rights of that body in matters of financial legislation. The chairman was Senator W. B. Ross. In a memorandum prepared by him and attached by the committee to its report is to be found the following:
To reject a supply bill might in olden times have been feasible, but today, with the functions of government so vast and complicated, it is unthinkable ... It would mean chaos. A supply bill should be passed as a matter of course by the Senate in almost any conceivable circumstances if it contains nothing but supply.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What year is that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is about thirty years ago. The quotation continues:
If other matters are inserted in the bill or "tacked to it" these should be struck out and be made into a separate bill or bills.
That is the whole point of this part of my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I am not necessarily objecting to any of the items to which I have referred. Some of them I would question, but some of them I am wholly in support of. But I think the position taken by that committee of the Senate thirty years ago, a position given endorsation by the fact that the Auditor General has now included it in the memorandum which he read before the Senate committee not long ago, is perfectly valid, namely, that you should not, if I may use those words, "tack to" a supply bill matters other than supply. If we want to give cabinet ministers or the leader of the opposition $2,000 a year motorcar allowance; if we want to have parliamentary assistants and pay them $4,000 extra a year; if we want to pay members of parliament and senators their full indemnity if they are absent more than fifteen days owing to illness; if we want to make special exceptions in the matter of appointments in the Department of Agriculture or by the Department of External Affairs-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or pay travelling expenses for Easter.

The Budget-Mr. Knowles

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If we want to pay travelling expenses for the Easter recess.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I agree; I fully agree to add that to my list. If we want to make any of these extra commitments; if we want to increase the salaries of the civil service commissioners; if we want to increase the salary of the secretary to the governor general; let us do it in the proper way, by a statute dealing with that specific proposal.
From time to time the Minister of Finance has criticized us in the opposition for the things that we have said about his budget, and he has asked us to look at it with a magnifying glass and find things that are wrong. Well, I hope I have satisfied him today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Only on procedure; you are taking the Tory line, that you agree with what is done, but that it is done the wrong way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. I think if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) paid attention to the first part of my speech, in which I dealt with the functions of a budget, and where I said his budget had fallen down, he will agree with me-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was referring to the latter part.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -that there is a wide difference between the so-called Tory line and our position with respect to budget policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was referring only to the latter part.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well then, the minister
wanted parliament to take time to examine the way in which they are building up the estimates, and asked for suggestions as to how they might be cut down. He got one answer from the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), and I have taken another approach. I have called as my chief witness, in support of the position I take, one whom he has properly described as a distinguished public servant, namely the Auditor General. His position is quite clear. He is the servant of parliament and his job is to help parliament protect its own rights. Let me say I have written to him at times about things that I thought were a little off colour, and I have had replies from him-on occasion-to the effect that I was wrong, and that the practice being followed was the proper one. In the matter about which I am speaking today, his views and mine agree.
In other words, I have complete confidence in the objectivity with respect to these matters of the Auditor General; and I think the

Minister of Finance should have the same confidence. Instead of brushing off the complaints I have made today he should take them more seriously. May I point out that in all of these I have been dealing with representations which the Auditor General made to a committee of the other place, but I have dealt with only one section of them. There are several other complaints he makes with respect to present practices in connection with estimates. If time makes it possible later in the session I shall discuss some of those other matters. At this time, however, I ask particularly that the government give serious consideration to the representations of the Auditor General, and that the practice of legislating by appropriations should be changed, and that the suggestions he has made should be accepted.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget which has been under consideration for some time, but under debate for only a few days, is in fact a statement of the way in which the government proposes to deal with the business of the country during the current year. The details are not before us in the budget for examination; and that, in itself, is a basic principle which must have some bearing upon a consideration of the budget. Those details will come before the house in the estimates, and in some cases will come before committees.
It is appropriate, however, to mention the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in presenting his budget which, in general terms, said in effect, "These are the expenditures we propose to make. We do not know any economies that can be practised. This level of approximately $2,400 million is going to continue as the lowest point we can expect to reach."
Within the estimates that I included are departments which propose to make very heavy expenditures. The department which will make the heaviest expenditures of any operating department of government is the Department of National Defence. In that case the estimates presented to us give no details which make it possible to understand anything more than the general purpose of the expenditures. That is merely an example of what we are encountering, in effect, in a number of other very important departments.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax-ton) has persistently resisted the request that his estimates be placed before a committee of the house, as has been done in the case of the Department of External Affairs and has been done in other cases. Now we have received the warning that the information is-

going to be fairly limited so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned. In a radio address last night the Minister of National Defence stated it was not possible to give the public information in regard to his department because the people who would like to know about it would be the Russians.
As has already been pointed out in the house, the estimates of the department of defence in the United Kingdom are placed before a committee, as are other estimates. As has also been pointed out, Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General, has on different occasions-and not only recently-indicated the necessity for improving the method of presenting accounts to the House of Commons, and of establishing a procedure which will restore to parliament effective control over the expenditure of public moneys.
I must confess I was surprised this afternoon to hear the Minister of Finance point out on more than one occasion that the Auditor General is not a lawyer-as though that in some way disqualified the Auditor General from expressing an opinion in regard to the propriety of some particular account, or as to the kind of account it might be. The Auditor General of Canada has been regarded with very high respect by both sides of the house, and his opinion has been regarded as a most reliable one. It has been assumed that when he makes a statement concerning accounts in one way or another, as to their being one kind or another, and that when he makes a statement as to the adequacy of procedure, he is doing so after having obtained whatever legal advice he might regard as necessary for that purpose. He would not be fulfilling his duties as Auditor General if he did not take steps to inform himself in regard to matters of that kind before stating his opinion, as he does. I have confidence, and I am sure most hon. members have confidence, that he is competent to make the statements he does make in his annual reports and on other occasions.
In respect of the Department of National Defence we are being asked to approve an expenditure of $425 million and to make commitments of $619 million. When we examine that item we must realize that a large part of this is made up of expenditures that under no conceivable circumstances could be regarded as secret in any way. Much of it is for clothing; much of it is for equipment; much of it is for buildings. And even that part of it devoted to military expenditures is for goods that are available, in their design and otherwise, to anyone who wishes to consult the ordinary textbooks open to the public. For that reason, these accounts along with others should be submitted to the investigation of a committee on estimates which in
The Budget-Mr. Drew turn would be subdivided into appropriate subcommittees to deal with the various departments.
If there is one thing essential to the effective conduct of the business of this house it is that all essential details be disclosed before members are asked to pass judgment on anything that is before them. That applies with particular force to the granting of those sums of money which in turn can be obtained only by the taxation of the people who are represented by all members here.
There is a simple and obvious reason why the government should seek to make full disclosure of every detail. After all, the government insists upon full details being disclosed by every individual. Every taxpayer must be ready to give the full details in regard to his affairs and it would seem only reasonable that the taxpayer who is going to pay the taxes should be assured of equally complete disclosure by the government of those expenditures which form the basis of that taxation.
In so far as this budget is concerned, it simply gives the broad picture and it is for that reason that amendments are not moved in regard to the detailed accounts as those amendments can always be moved at another time. The amendment proposed by the party to which I belong indicates our views as to the way in which this budget fails to present a proper approach to the problems that are ahead of us. The amendment that was introduced, after the usual introductory word, states:
This house regrets that the policies ol the government, as announced by the Minister of Finance,
(1)	make higher taxation inevitable;
(2)	make no adequate attempt to eliminate extravagance and avoid unnecessary expenditure; and
(3)	make no provision for a program of national development, without which there can be no hope of a reduction of taxation and the present high cost of living.
The statement that the budget makes higher taxation inevitable is based upon the obvious fact that if any of the things are to be done which the government has undertaken to do and which it has not yet done, there is no way of carrying out those undertakings except by higher taxation. Furthermore there will of necessity be higher taxation in order to meet our requirements unless production continues at the level of last year.
The second point is that the budget makes no adequate attempt to eliminate extravagance and avoid unnecessary expenditure. The Minister of Finance has an utterly meaningless interjection which he makes from time to time: "You approve of what we do, but you do not like the way we do it." That statement in itself reflects upon his sense

The Budget-Mr. Drew of responsibility in dealing with this budget and with all it entails. The Minister of Finance comes forward with this budget, which means that the people of Canada will be called upon to pay $2,400 million in taxes, and indicates no way in which any attempt is to be made to increase the efficiency of government, to avoid duplication of services and to reduce unnecessary expenditures in cases where that can be done.
The Minister of Finance says very often, "Show us where we can save money; show us where this can be done." At the same time we are presented with estimates about which the details are not available, and in the case of the largest of these it is said that we cannot get the details because some other country might like to know what they are. There is not a member of this house who does not know of a case where there could be improvement in efficiency and a reduction in the duplication of services, with advantage both to the business of government and to the civil service which is handling the business of government.
Even if there were no such knowledge available we have this simple problem before us. Because of the commitments of war it was necessary and inevitable that there should be a great expansion of government services. In the very nature of that expansion new tasks were undertaken without the time being given that would ordinarily be given to organizing activities of that sort. Any ordinary business which had been called upon to expand in that unexpected and sudden manner would have put experts in to examine its accounts, to examine its structural organization and to suggest improvements in the way of doing business. Any ordinary business that did not carry out some such procedure would be headed for financial trouble. The methods of ordinary business should apply to the business of government, although I agree that they have not been applied and in many cases are not intended to apply.
One thing that should concern every member is the fact that statements have been frankly made by those who are associated with certain services connected with the government that ordinary business methods do not apply. Another thing that should cause concern is the statement that ordinary methods of accounting cannot be put into effect. During the last few years there has been an increasing emphasis everywhere on the necessity of efficient cost accounting. The cost-accounting mind is

completely absent from any approach to the business of government which has been displayed in this house.
The only way that this broadly expanded business of government can be examined and brought to the ultimate efficiency is to do what any efficient business, large or small, would do, have the whole business of government examined by experts and have recommendations made as to how the whole business of government can be made more efficient and how the business of the people can be brought back under the control of parliament itself.
I have already indicated that I intend to bring this subject up on another occasion. For that reason I shall not discuss it in more detail today because members of the house will have an opportunity to express their opinions upon it. But I emphasize to every member the great need for an examination of the whole business of government as one of the factors in the stand we are taking with other democracies against the threat of communist imperialism today. The efficiency of democratic governments is going to measure to a very large extent the way in which they will maintain their strength during that period which has been described as the cold war. The winning of that cold war, without its ever turning into a shooting war, depends to a considerable degree upon the extent to which we can convince the thirteen men in the Kremlin that the business of the democracies is so efficiently conducted that there is no chance of any danger to their economic structure in the years ahead. For that very reason, as a part of the strength of democracy itself in Canada, we should follow a course that will bring to its maximum efficiency the whole business of government which is the business of the people themselves.
The third point made in the amendment is that there is no provision for a program of national development without which there can be no hope of a reduction of taxation and the present high cost of living. Nowhere in the budget statement is there any suggestion of carrying on any of those activities which would help to expand many of our natural opportunities in Canada in a way which would help to expand production and also help to support a very much larger population. Although it was denied a short time ago, it can no longer be denied that we face a period of decreasing prices for the products of Canada, and it can no longer be denied that unemployment on a very substantial scale is already here.

When those facts are mentioned there are those who say that anyone who mentions unemployment or lower prices for basic products is showing a lack of faith in Canada. The very opposite is the case. We have faith in Canada and its resources, and we do not believe that there should be idle resources in Canada when there are unemployed people who could be working on their development.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about gas lines?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very glad gas lines have been mentioned. Canada has available enormous resources of power in the form of electricity, gas and oil. The way to create employment in Canada is to make sure that the first use of those resources is for Canadians themselves. That is what we have been emphasizing and that is what we have been asking. In the past few years discoveries challenging the imagination have been made in oil, gas and iron, as well as titanium and other basic minerals and commodities, all of which can be the basis of a vastly increased population in Canada. By all means let us export the surpluses that we cannot use here up to the point that such export is consistent with our long-term advantage, but also let us be careful that in exporting raw materials we do not to some extent endanger our own future by limiting the amount that may be available at some future time when our population will be very much greater than it is today. There are some kinds of production and export that we can carry on to the maximum without impairment of our strength in any way.
So long as our soil is maintained, so long as conservation methods are practised, there is no reason why we should not produce all that can be produced from our soil for both domestic consumption and export. In the case of such products as those manufactured from the forest wealth of the country, so long as careful conservation is practised and cutting is limited to a point that assures a perpetual crop, there is no reason why we should not export all that we can over and above our own requirements. A different situation, however, arises as to such resources as nickel, copper, lead, zinc, iron, wasting assets of that kind. A very large part of our buoyancy has depended upon exports of these products. I am not suggesting there should be no export but I am suggesting that in all these cases we should seek to expand in every way we can the use of these mineral and other resources in our own country for the employment of Canadians.
There is unemployment today. There are men who desperately want work. There are
The Budget-Mr. Drew resources which can be developed by the government as great national ventures without imposing new tax burdens upon the taxpayers. These resources would produce new power and create new producing capacity from one end of the country to the other. When we express regret that the budget statement indicates no provision for anything of that kind we are combining that with the speech from the throne because it would be within those two speeches that any indication of such action would be disclosed.
We have great confidence in the future of this country. The population any country can support is determined by the food it produces, by the material it can produce for the construction of homes and other necessary buildings, and by the work available for the people. These things are to be found in Canada far beyond the requirements of the present population. We could feed several times the number now living here. We could heat homes in this country with various fuels that are available; and we have the raw materials with which to build homes or other buildings. It is not necessary to determine what the exact figure may be as long as we are confident that we can support that larger population. If we can, then whatever we do to develop new power resources, and resources of other kinds, will assure a substantially larger population in the years to come, over which the burden of our accumulated debts can be distributed. In that way alone can there be a general reduction of taxation. It is perfectly true that a very large part of the tax burden of this country is the result of the part we played in two world wars. That will be a continuing debt for a long time to come; but one way to ease that burden is to do what may be reasonable to spread the carrying charges of that obligation over a larger number of people.
Coming to the subamendment now before us, I see that it refers to development and an increase in production, with which we can most certainly agree. In the second paragraph, however, it regrets that the government makes no provision for increased national production through economic planning, public control of investment and public ownership of monopolistic industries; then it goes on to make further statements. Economic planning must be understood as those words are meant in this case; and in this case economic planning means economic shackles. I recognize that probably those who put forward this suggestion do not believe that yet, but in too many places in the world there have been convincing demonstrations of the fact that the intervention of government in the general economy of a country has limiting
1922	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew rather than expanding results. Also I cannot imagine anything that would be more fatal to the future of a country so relatively undeveloped as Canada as control of investment by government and government doctrinaires.
I do not need to emphasize what the control of investment by government would mean. It would simply mean that the development of anything in this country would depend upon the judgment of some official of the government as to whether or not a particular investment should be made. Nothing would be more certain to prevent the investment of risk capital, which is essential to the full development of our great resources which are capable of so much greater use than that to which they are now being put, right from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
As for the public ownership of monopolistic industries, I would point out that this is a very loose term. Monopolistic industries may mean almost anything, as it has in Saskatchewan. There industries have been taken over for public development, in one case because there was a dispute within the industry; in another case because the government did not like what was being done; and in a number of other cases for no reason that had any relationship to a monopolistic position. On the experience of what has happened in the one case where it has been openly tried in this country, certainly I am convinced that this would impose a measure of control and possibly punitive action, if it could be exercised by those putting it forward, which would be dangerous indeed to the future of this country, and for that reason the party to which I belong will not support the subamendment though the first paragraph and the last part of the second paragraph contain statements with which we could certainly agree.
Having made these observations I only repeat that I feel sure there are those who mistakenly believe some of these ideas would be sound; but if practices of this kind could be justified at all, I can think of no time when they would be less justified and more unwise than at the present, with the vast opportunities that are opening before us today.
This budget debate will be followed by consideration of the estimates, and at that time many details can be examined to such extent as they are available. There is one subject I would put forward at this time, however, since it is something that cannot be dealt with effectively on the estimates-that is the desirability of taking appropriate steps to avoid duplication as between departments of the dominion and provincial governments.


Many of the services being given today could be provided very much more efficiently if a decision were made as to which government should handle a particular subject and what device should be employed for raising the necessary money. Then the whole business could be handled by one department, instead of being divided among one department at Ottawa and ten provincial departments, all dealing with some aspects of the same subject. That applies with particular force to the department of health, and it applies to the departments dealing with lands and forests and minerals. It applies to a number of other departments, and a careful approach to the broad problem of public expenditure would undoubtedly find ways in which substantial reductions could be made at one level or another, the dominion, provincial or municipal, with increased efficiency and with more effective contact with those who are served. That is not something which, at the moment, can be included in the terms of this budget. On this occasion I am simply putting it forward as a suggestion, which is parallel to the suggestion I have already made, that by an examination of the structure of government itself the duplication of services as between government departments, and within departments, could be avoided.
These observations have been made, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that, whatever the result of this vote may be, and I am not making any suggestion that the motion before the house will not be supported by the majority of the house, when that time comes I am still hopeful that parliament will be ready to accept suggestions, and to seek ways by which the business of the people can be brought fully under the control and supervision of the people's representatives. I am sure that to the extent that every member on both sides of the house is prepared to approach the problem in that way, we shall all be making a contribution to the development of Canada in the years ahead.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time on behalf of the people of Davenport, whom I have the honour to represent. The constituency of Davenport is situated in what was formerly known as the town of York. It is now known from coast to coast, yes even across the seas, as Liberal Toronto. The people of Davenport are ordinary people, and most of them, like myself, are forced to work for a living for reasons that are entirely beyond their control. We in Davenport do not claim high mountains, broad rivers, great mines, or any of the other natural legacies so proudly enumerated by the people of other areas in this great dominion. We do, however, have great respect for

my illustrious predecessor, Dr. J. R. MacNicol, who is a great Canadian, a fine gentleman, and one who does not wish to damn anything -with the probable exception of the south Saskatchewan river.
The people of Davenport are sensible people, and most of them do not make unreasonable demands on government. They only seek a reasonably buoyant economy, one which will provide employment and opportunity for individual initiative, along with a certain amount of collective security to take care of those hazards which are handled so well by means of the insurance principle. It is because of those modest requirements, and the way that they have been and are still being taken care of by the present administration, that I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance on the consistent economic policy he has followed in the presentation of his several budgets. It must have required a great deal of intestinal fortitude to present the first two budgets containing the extremely high taxes and restraints that were necessary to control the inflationary tendencies of that time. They were definitely unpopular, and justifiably so in the minds of some people who are prone to criticize.
Then, last year a much more pleasant task devolved upon the minister in that, still in line with his policy, it was necessary to relax some of the restrictions and reduce taxes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The 27th of June.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend questions the motive behind last year's budget, but we will not get into a discussion of that. It is possible to kill two birds with one stone, but what I am going to say about this particular budget, regardless of what anyone may think of it, is that it is consistent with the principles set out by the Minister of Finance. This afternoon we have heard people bemoaning the fact that there is some unemployment, and that some people are apprehensive of the future. Before I proceed let me say that last year's budget has been responsible for more production, and more employment, than anyone on the other side of the house is probably willing to give it credit for. If those reductions had not taken place we might have encountered a slight recession, as is the case in the United States.
This year we have a budget which is described by hon. members opposite as a stand-pat budget, and I think rightly so. Conditions in the country today warrant that type of a budget. It is consistent with the policy of preventing the cost of living from rising any further, and at the same time maintaining employment and industry in
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer its present buoyant state. I am sorry the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) is not in his seat, because the other night he made a statement that this was the end of cyclical budgeting. I do not know whether or not the name means anything in particular, but so far as this budget policy is concerned, I do not think it is the end. So far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, it is probably only the beginning of a new phase in the consistent policy so ably initiated by him a few years ago.
The opposition has presented an amendment showing, want of confidence in the minister. They have mentioned three things they think ought to have been done which have not been done, or vice versa, as the case may be; they change their minds so often it does not matter which way you look at it. They bemoan the fact that the things that have been done cause higher taxation. I was looking through a booklet of the campaign speeches and pledges made by the leader of the opposition prior to this date of June 27 which is thrown at us from the opposite side of the house, in which he promises all sorts of things such as canals, highways, bridges, and old age pensions. I should like to quote one phrase from that booklet; "-far beyond any pledge of social security put forward by any other government in the history of this country."
What sort of broad statement that is, 1 do not know.

National development is also in line with the minister's procedure of sound budgeting. At the present time projects are being carried forward as fast as they can be absorbed. If you read the forecast tabled in this house you will find that this year the capital expenditure will probably be the highest in the history of the Canadian economy. Most of it is relegated to two or three particular types of construction and development. Most of the things which hon. members opposite

The Budget-Mr. Hellyer have suggested we should have done are things which would compete with the things being done, to the extent that the inflationary spiral would start again, with higher and higher prices; and you would be right back throwing at us the fact that things were getting out of hand and our money was being further depreciated, and so on.
The conclusion to these few remarks is,
I think, Mr. Speaker, that they do not know just what to ask for and do not know just what to complain about but because of their honourable status as His Majesty's loyal opposition they have to take some position. speechtext: Look at the Liberal benches; they are half empty.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), made a statement which I found most interesting. He mentioned the freedom that has brought us as far as we have come. I believe that is worthy of consideration. At the same time the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) recently made the statement, during a comment on a speech made by some other hon. member opposite, that he thought the situation could be handled by the same processes we have always used; by carrying on with exactly the same methods and techniques that we had used during the past generations and decades. Unfortunately, I do not believe that is true, and I know that the . Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) does not think it is true or he would not have initiated this consistent policy which has been called cyclical budgeting; you can call it what you like.
The first great reason why it is not so and why the leader of the opposition is not on solid ground is that some of what he calls the natural laws no longer apply in our economy. What have been referred to as


booms are usually artificial booms; and busts are, by the same definition, in many respects artificial too. I have not the time to go into the background of this; but, as you all know, in ancient days most of the economies were of the nature of one or two products; and if you had a natural failure, by immediate consequence you then had a depressed state. There has been a gradual tendency away from this and we have developed exceedingly complex societies, complex economic relationships, and a degree of specialization of labour which was never previously dreamed of. If you average all the cycles, all the moods of men, all the lack of rain in one area of the country offset by rain in the other, you find that the potential production of a diversified economy like our own does not change a great deal from one year to the next, except by natural increase.
The leader of the opposition would lead us to believe that if we just sort of let things go their own natural course-I think he might favour returning to the gold standard or something-it would all right itself and pretty soon we would have a new equilibrium which would have all of the necessary requirements to produce full employment and an extremely buoyant economy. Unfortunately this is not true either, and it is due to a natural process which has developed during the last two hundred years. We started with small industries. For natural reasons those have integrated and have become larger and larger for the sake of efficiency. Every year we have more industries, more products and more classes of produce in a category which could be said to be of a semi-rigid or rigid price nature. They are prices set by arbitrary decision and which do not obey the laws of supply and demand-one of the leader of the opposition's natural laws. A few years ago we had more commodities which fell in the natural price law category but the numbers are diminishing, and we now find ourselves in a complex economy in which we have a predominantly private enterprise, semi-rigid price structure. We still have some commodities in the free enterprise free competitive price category which obey the law of supply and demand.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before I take my seat, I think I will just close by saying that I have every confidence in both the administration and the Minister of Finance and his officials, to maintain equilibrium, to maintain our purchasing power and to keep in this country that degree of economic buoyancy which is necessary to provide ample employment, and an increasingly higher standard of living for those apostles who keep interrupting with their gloomy remarks from the opposite side of the house. I have every confidence that there will be no depression in this country. A depression is not necessary.

We do not intend to have one. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if hon. members opposite would devote their time and talents
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer to an effort to develop new industries so as to provide employment in exploiting the natural resources of the country, we might make appreciable progress toward full nationhood, and in the process enable immigrants in larger numbers to join with us in building Canada into that still greater nation which I am sure we all fervently hope it will one day become. As a closing remark, Mr. Speaker, I should think that this all ties in with something else which is of extreme interest to most people at the present time, and that is that if we can break this one thing, this business cycle, we shall have for all time disproved the Marxist theory and, in the words of Woodrow Wilson, made the world safe for democracy.
